questions.prompt: Why could analysts map building damage from the Eaton Fire with Sentinel-1 before crews could safely enter the area?
choices: Radar satellites send their own signal, which passes through smoke and cloud
Radar satellites take color photos with very high resolution
Residents uploaded photos of their homes to the satellite
Radar measures air temperature, which shows where buildings burned
questions.explain: Radar is an active sensor: it sends out microwaves and records what bounces back, so smoke and cloud don't block it.

questions.prompt: After an earthquake in remote mountains, rescuers ask where to search first. What does a GIS do to help?
choices: Combines layers such as shaking intensity, buildings, population, and open roads
Shows a single photo of the epicenter
Predicts the exact time of the next earthquake
Lists the names of the people who live nearby
questions.explain: No single map answers the question. Overlaying several layers finds the places that meet several conditions at once.

questions.prompt: "One flooded home, one county, the whole Gulf Coast" describes which of the four questions about a geographic problem?
questions.explain: Scale asks whether the problem looks different at different levels of geographic detail.

questions.prompt: "Hours of storm surge, years of rebuilding" describes which of the four questions about a geographic problem?
questions.explain: Time asks whether the consequences are short-term, long-term, or both.

questions.prompt: "Are we advancing scientific knowledge or solving a practical problem?" is the question of:
questions.explain: Purpose separates research (better surge models) from practice (faster evacuations).

questions.prompt: Put the four questions that define a geographic problem in the order the chapter gives them.
questions.explain: Scale, time, space, and purpose. Together they describe the where, when, how big, and why of a problem.

questions.prompt: Mapping the extent of the Deepwater Horizon oil spill each day mainly answered which kind of question?
choices: How things have changed over a century
What would happen if a bridge closed
questions.explain: The simplest GIS question is where is it? Daily maps of the oil drove fishing closures and cleanup.

questions.prompt: Comparing satellite images of the same coast before and after the 2004 tsunami is called change ___.
questions.explain: Change detection compares images or maps of one place at two times.

questions.prompt: How does routing software find the fastest route?
choices: It treats roads as a network of segments with travel times and searches for the lowest-cost path
It draws a straight line between the two places
It picks the route with the fewest turns
It asks other drivers which way they went
questions.explain: Route optimization is network analysis: each segment has a cost, and the software finds the path with the lowest total.

questions.prompt: Choosing the best place for a new fire station is an example of:
questions.explain: Site selection uses GIS to find the best location for a facility.

questions.prompt: "Where is there flat, forested land within 1 km of a road and outside the floodplain?" is which kind of GIS question?
questions.explain: A condition question asks where the places are that meet a set of conditions.

questions.prompt: "What happens to traffic if this bridge closes?" is which kind of GIS question?
questions.explain: Modeling questions ask what would happen under a scenario.

questions.prompt: GIS sits at the overlap of which two fields?
questions.explain: Geography asks where things are and why; computer science provides data, algorithms, and software.

questions.prompt: Bolstad defines a GIS as a ___-based system to aid in the collection, maintenance, storage, analysis, output, and distribution of spatial data and information.
questions.explain: The definition says computer-based, which is why John Snow's paper map is debatable as a GIS.

questions.prompt: Which of these is spatial data?
choices: A list of student ID numbers
questions.explain: Spatial data are tied to a location on Earth.

questions.prompt: What did John Snow's 1854 map show?
choices: Cholera deaths clustered around the Broad Street water pump
That cholera spread through bad air
Where the city's sewers drained into the river
questions.explain: Snow mapped deaths and pumps. The deaths clustered around the Broad Street pump, and its handle was removed.

questions.prompt: By Bolstad's definition, John Snow's hand-drawn map is a GIS, because it has spatial data and analysis.
questions.explain: Bolstad's definition says computer-based, and Snow had no computer. It does everything else a GIS does, which is why it is a good one to argue about.

questions.prompt: Which component sits at the center of the five components of a GIS?
questions.explain: Data are the center; hardware, software, people, and procedures surround them.

questions.prompt: Which is NOT one of the five components of a GIS?
questions.explain: The five are data, hardware, software, people, and procedures.

questions.prompt: Agreed methods and workflows that make results reliable and repeatable are the GIS component called:
questions.explain: Procedures make sure two analysts with the same data and question get the same answer.

questions.prompt: Pen and paper can count as GIS hardware.
questions.explain: Hardware can be as simple as pen and paper or as complex as GPS units, drones, and servers.

questions.prompt: Building a better model of where wildfires will spread is an example of:
questions.explain: GIScience is the research behind the tools. Mapping today's perimeter would be a GISystem task.

questions.prompt: Mapping today's fire perimeter is a GIScience research question.
questions.explain: It is a practical task done with a GISystem.

questions.prompt: The geographer Michael ___ coined the term geographic information science in 1992.
questions.explain: Goodchild argued that the hard problems of GIS are scientific questions in their own right.

questions.prompt: Why is CAD software spatial but not geographic?
choices: Its drawings aren't tied to places on Earth
questions.explain: Geographic means locations on or near Earth's surface, with coordinates and projections.

questions.prompt: Which word is often used as a synonym for geographic, especially in industry and government?
questions.explain: For example, the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency.

questions.prompt: Roger Tomlinson, often called the father of GIS, led which early system?
questions.explain: CGIS was built in the 1960s to inventory land across Canada.

questions.prompt: Ian McHarg's 1969 book *Design with Nature* popularized which technique?
questions.explain: McHarg stacked transparent maps of soils, slope, water, and land use to find suitable places to build.

questions.prompt: Put these events in the history of GIS in order, earliest first.
Put the steps of the GIS process in order, starting from the physical world.
questions.explain: Data come in from the world, and decisions go back out to it, starting the cycle again.

questions.prompt: In the GIS process cycle, where does GIS connect to the physical world?
choices: Where data come in and where decisions go back out
questions.explain: The two links to the real world are data collection (in) and decisions and action (out).

questions.prompt: QGIS is free, open source, and runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
questions.explain: ArcGIS Pro, by contrast, is commercial and runs on Windows only.

questions.prompt: ArcGIS Pro runs on Windows, Mac, and Linux.
questions.explain: ArcGIS Pro runs only on Windows. QGIS runs on all three.

questions.prompt: "Which neighborhoods have less access to hospitals?" is which kind of GIS question?
questions.explain: Accessibility questions measure distance or travel time to a service.

questions.prompt: "How has forest cover changed in the Blue Ridge Mountains after Hurricane Helene?" needs:
choices: Data from more than one time
Only a map of today's forests
questions.explain: A change question compares the same place at two or more times.

questions.prompt: What was redlining?
choices: Grading neighborhoods as risky for lending on maps, which denied credit to many Black and immigrant neighborhoods
Marking fire perimeters on a map
A method for correcting map projections
questions.explain: The 1930s Home Owners' Loan Corporation maps shaped lending for decades, and their effects are still visible.

questions.prompt: Removing names from phone location data is always enough to keep people anonymous.
questions.explain: A few location points are often enough to find where someone lives and works, and so who they are.
